trigger: poc-generator PoC test/poc-M-02-retirement-strands-buffer.t.sol (10 passed, real NudgeStreamer + real BatchNFTMinterMultiToken) partially REFUTED the M-02 raise as I framed it.

selfCorrection.whatIClaimed: In the prior audit I wrote that the orphaned streamer buffer is 'permanently unrescuable', has 'no rescue path from any address', and that retirement means the buffer is 'permanently unrecoverable by anyone'. I ranked L-02 up to Medium on the value-leak limb of C4 Medium on that basis.
selfCorrection.whatIsTrue: The buffer IS recoverable. I verified the refutation independently in source rather than accepting it: NudgeStreamer._settle (NudgeStreamer.sol:182-191) ends in `IERC20(token).safeTransfer(recipient, settled)` — it PUSHES to the recipient. It is not a pull. Both registerStream (:118, settle-before-reset) and collectNudge (:145, settle-before-deposit) call _settle before doing their own work, and _accrued caps at the full buffer once the window has elapsed. So ANY call that triggers a settle shoves the entire buffer into the retired sink, where rescueERC20 (BatchNFTMinterMultiToken.sol:383, explicitly still callable while paused) recovers it. The PoC demonstrates both routes: registerStream recovered 4,108,708,527, and a 1-wei collectNudge by an arbitrary address does the same.
selfCorrection.howIGotItWrong: I enumerated the streamer's EXTERNAL function surface (registerStream, collectNudge, pullPendingStream, pendingStream, Ownable), correctly found no rescue/sweep/withdraw, correctly established that pullPendingStream is msg.sender-keyed — and then concluded 'unrecoverable'. That conclusion does not follow from those premises. I checked which functions exist and who may call them, but never checked the TRANSFER DIRECTION inside the settle helper that three of those four functions invoke. A push-to-recipient primitive means the recipient does not need to pull, so msg.sender-keying of pullPendingStream is not the constraint I treated it as.
selfCorrection.theEvidenceWasAlreadyInFrontOfMe: This is the part I want on the record. Tier-3 line 148 stated the buffer is 'permanently in transit to the intended recipient' and line 144-146 said registerStream 'settles at the old rate and re-spreads the same buffer'. I read both, and I read the word 'settles' as bookkeeping rather than as an outbound transfer. I then over-generalized test_P2_D, which asserts only that the OWNER's balance is unchanged across registerStream — true, and NOT the same proposition as 'no address can recover it'. The classifier and the Tier-3 author had this right; I introduced the error while arguing they were under-calling. I withdraw the claim without reservation.
selfCorrection.processNote: I asked for this PoC in order to convict my own raise. It refuted it instead. That is the mechanism working correctly, and the corrected finding is materially better than either the classifier's original or my raise — see rationaleCorrection under M-02/L-02 below.

answersToCoordinator.question: 1. Does M-02 still hold at Medium when reframed as an operational hazard / false-assurance defect rather than permanent fund destruction?
answersToCoordinator.ruling: NO. I WITHDRAW the raise. M-02 returns to LOW.
answersToCoordinator.reasoning: I raised it on the value-leak limb of C4 Medium — 'value leak with stated assumptions and external requirements'. The PoC removes the leak. Not by making it conditional or unlikely, but by demonstrating the value arrives at its intended recipient and is recoverable there. When the specific limb invoked is factually refuted, the raise must be withdrawn. The other Medium limb (protocol function/availability) does not apply either: SYA keeps working throughout, new claims fund the new pair normally, and nothing about the protocol's operation is impaired.
answersToCoordinator.downgradeIsAffirmativelyJustified: Per the symmetry rule a downgrade needs an affirmative basis and must never be chosen to make a report look calmer. The basis here is the strongest kind available — the loss mechanism I asserted does not exist, proven constructively against the real contracts. This is not 'most findings are Medium' pressure; it is a refuted premise.
answersToCoordinator.notABorderlineKeepHigher: I considered whether the 'when genuinely borderline, keep the higher severity' rule applies and concluded it does not. See lossVsOpsHazardAnalysis below — the discriminators point one way, not two.

answersToCoordinator.question: 2. Does the correction change the M-01 raise?
answersToCoordinator.ruling: NO. M-01 stands at MEDIUM, unchanged. Confirmed by re-examination, not assumed.
answersToCoordinator.reasoning: The refutation is entirely about the RECOVERABILITY OF VALUE sitting in a NudgeStreamer buffer. M-01 is an AVAILABILITY finding with no value component: setRewardToken (StableYieldAccumulator.sol:417-420) re-keys the (nudge, rewardToken) stream lookup so that every claim() carrying a payable nudge share reverts NudgeStreamer__NotRegistered (0xd62cbfe8). The _settle push semantics are irrelevant to it — the revert happens at the registration check in collectNudge (:143, `if (s.duration == 0) revert NudgeStreamer__NotRegistered()`) BEFORE any settle is reached, so no push occurs and none could help. Nothing in the PoC touches the stream-key mismatch, the missing event, the closed-enumeration NatSpec defect, or the ordered cross-contract cure.
answersToCoordinator.crossCheck: I also re-tested whether the push semantics create an unnoticed self-cure for M-01 — i.e. whether some settle path could re-arm the broken key. It cannot: _settle never writes s.duration, and the only two sites that set duration are registerStream (onlyOwner) and the constructor. The brick requires an explicit owner registerStream on the new pair, exactly as filed. M-01's ledger-consistency argument (ledger M-01, a lesser owner-omission footgun, is ranked Medium in this same project) is also untouched.

answersToCoordinator.question: 3. Does it change the ruling that L-03 stays Low on anti-double-counting grounds, given the dollars are recoverable-but-un-redirectable rather than lost?
answersToCoordinator.ruling: L-03 STAYS LOW — but my stated reasoning for it is now partly obsolete and must be replaced. The anti-double-counting argument is no longer needed and should be dropped.
answersToCoordinator.reasoning: I had justified L-03's Low by saying 'L-02 Medium carries the loss, L-03 Low carries the magnitude, raising both would double-count the same dollars.' With L-02 back at Low there is no Medium to double-count against, so that scaffolding falls away. L-03 does not need it: it now stands on the ORIGINAL classifier rationale, which the PoC has independently strengthened. The Tier-3 framing 'permanently in transit to the intended recipient, not lost' is not a euphemism — it is now demonstrated against the real contracts under the adversarial retirement scenario I constructed to break it. L-03 is a steady-state work-in-progress float whose root cause is out of scope (NudgeStreamer.sol:150-153 full-duration rate recompute, parked as PARK-001). Low is correct.
answersToCoordinator.whatSurvivesFromMyCorrection: One amendment to L-03 stands: its escalation trigger (b) 'the sink is retired and never flushes again' must still be reclassified from EXCEPTIONAL to EVIDENCED, because SWING-003 (sink retirement is documented, twice-scripted ops practice) is untouched by the refutation. What changes is the CONSEQUENCE attached to that trigger: it is now 'requires unprompted manual recovery', not 'permanent loss'. The trigger is real; its payload is smaller than I said.
answersToCoordinator.irony: The PoC I commissioned to prove L-03's dead-end was fatal instead produced the best available evidence that L-03's Low was correctly reasoned all along.

answersToCoordinator.question: 4. Final label set.
answersToCoordinator.ruling: 0 High, 1 Medium, 7 Low, 1 QA — total 9, one-to-one with the sanitized inputs, zero dropped.

lossVsOpsHazardAnalysis.question: Is 'recoverable only by unprompted manual intervention' closer to economic loss or to an operational hazard?
lossVsOpsHazardAnalysis.standingRuleCheck: The coordinator correctly notes the codebase-family rule that merely MISALLOCATED value is not economic loss, and correctly notes it does not automatically apply here because econ-scanner established this leg is claimer-paid CONSIDERATION, not externally-derived yield (memoryRef externally-derived-yield-opportunity-cost-not-loss, ruled INAPPLICABLE to this leg — I concur with that ruling and do not disturb it). So ordinary stranding WOULD be real loss. The question is whether this is stranding.
lossVsOpsHazardAnalysis.verdict: OPERATIONAL HAZARD, not loss. The discriminators point one way.
discriminators: NO EXPIRY — recovery is available indefinitely. The buffer does not decay, expire, or become harder to reach with time. Nothing forecloses the remedy.
NO ADVERSARY — no party can take the funds, race for them, or block recovery. There is no competing claim on them.
NO DEGRADATION — the amount is static once claims stop; there is no bleed.

RECOVERY IS CHEAP AND NEARLY PERMISSIONLESS — a 1-wei collectNudge from ANY address triggers the push. It does not require the owner, a quorum, a timelock, or a deployment. The de-whitelist variant blocks the owner's registerStream lever but leaves the outsider route intact.

THE MISSING INGREDIENT IS KNOWLEDGE, AND THIS REPORT SUPPLIES IT — the sole reason funds would sit is that nobody knows to act. A finding that documents the remedy converts the hazard into a checklist item. Loss that a report can undo by being written was not loss.
lossVsOpsHazardAnalysis.counterweightConsidered: The strongest argument for Medium: if nobody ever performs the intervention, the economic outcome is indistinguishable from loss, and the runbook actively tells the operator everything is clean. I weighed this seriously — it is the reason this is a judgement call rather than a formality. I reject it because C4's value-leak limb requires the leak to occur, and here the leak is contingent on a FURTHER assumption (that the remedy is never exercised) which this very finding defeats. Stacking a contingency on top of a contingency to reach Medium is precisely the over-severing the pipeline rejects, and it would be my second framing error on the same finding.
lossVsOpsHazardAnalysis.whatThisIsNot: This is emphatically NOT a case of talking a finding down to keep the report calm. The finding gets STRONGER in substance under the correction — see below. Only the label moves.

revisedFinding.verdict: RAISE WITHDRAWN — returns to Low, with a materially corrected rationale
revisedFinding.revisedTitle: The documented sink-retirement gate is structurally blind to the NudgeStreamer buffer and returns a false all-clear
revisedFinding.reframe: From 'retirement permanently destroys up to 30 days of nudge donations' to 'retirement certifies clean while ~30 days of nudge donations sit outside the gate's field of view, recoverable only by an unprompted manual cross-contract intervention that the runbook gives the operator no reason to perform'.
whatThePocProved: The gate is blind and returns a false all-clear — STRONGER than I filed it. Even an operator who runs the documented drain and recovers 496.2 USDC via rescueERC20 still gets `require(IERC20(USDC).balanceOf(OLD_BATCH_MINTER) == 0)` passing while 4,108 USDC sits in the streamer (test_M02_01).
The outstanding amount converges to donationRate x duration: observed 14,982,961,180 vs 15,000,000,000 expected, ~30 days of donations, with the gate still reading zero (test_M02_04).

All three severing mechanisms independently kill the DESIGNED automatic delivery route — pause, de-whitelist, zero-streamer (test_M02_02a/02b/02c). The classifier's original Low rationale ('batchMint is permissionless so anyone can drain it indefinitely') is therefore FALSE at retirement, which is exactly when it matters.
NudgeStreamer has no rescue/sweep/withdraw surface — 10 signatures probed — and pullPendingStream is msg.sender-keyed, with 4 non-recipient callers confirmed as no-ops (test_M02_03).

The buffer is UN-REDIRECTABLE: registering the replacement sink's stream leaves the old buffer keyed to the retired pair. Value cannot be moved to the new sink; it can only be pushed to the old one and rescued from there.
whatThePocRefuted: 'Permanently unrecoverable / no rescue path from any address' — FALSE. _settle PUSHES (NudgeStreamer.sol:186).
registerStream pushes the buffer to the retired sink; rescueERC20 then recovers it — 4,108,708,527 recovered (test_M02_R1).
A 1-wei collectNudge by ANY address achieves the same push (test_M02_R2).

De-whitelist retirement blocks the owner's registerStream lever, since registerStream re-checks isNudgeToken (NudgeStreamer.sol:112-114) — leaving the outsider 1-wei route as the remaining path (test_M02_R3).

rationaleCorrection.note: The label returns to where the classifier had it, but this is NOT a vindication of the classifier's reasoning, and the finding must not be written up as though nothing happened. Three positions have now been held, and the third is the correct one:
rationaleCorrection.classifierOriginal: Low, because 'batchMint is permissionless and its step-3.5 flush loop runs unconditionally, so any caller can drain the orphan indefinitely.' REFUTED by test_M02_02a/02b/02c — every automatic route dies at retirement. Right label, wrong reason.
rationaleCorrection.myRaise: Medium, because the buffer is permanently unrecoverable. REFUTED by test_M02_R1/R2 — _settle pushes. Wrong label, wrong reason.
rationaleCorrection.correctPosition: Low, because although every AUTOMATIC delivery route dies at retirement, a manual push (registerStream by the owner, or a 1-wei collectNudge by anyone) still delivers the buffer to the retired sink, where rescueERC20 recovers it in full. The defect is the FALSE ASSURANCE — the gate certifies clean while the value is outstanding and while every automatic route to it is dead — not the destruction of funds.
rationaleCorrection.whyThisMatters: The corrected rationale is what makes the recommendation actionable and correctly scoped. Under the classifier's reasoning there is nothing much to fix, because organic batchMint demand supposedly handles it. Under mine, the fix would have been framed as preventing catastrophic loss. Under the correct reading, the fix is precise: extend the gate, and document the manual recovery route so the operator knows it exists. That is a Low-severity fix for a Low-severity defect — but it is a fix that neither prior position would have specified correctly.

revisedFinding.law3Ruling: IN SCOPE and unchanged as a non-obvious owner footgun. The surprise test is met decisively: an operator runs the documented retirement, the script's own safety assertion passes, and ~30 days of donations are outstanding in a contract the gate never looks at, with every automatic delivery route now dead. A competent, non-malicious owner would be surprised. Law 3 requires this be reported at honest severity — and honest severity here is Low.
recommendation: PRIMARY (unchanged, and still the highest-value deliverable of this audit): extend the retirement gate at ReplaceBatchNFTMinter.s.sol:486 and MigrateBatchNFTMinter.s.sol:500 from `require(IERC20(USDC).balanceOf(OLD_BATCH_MINTER) == 0)` to additionally assert `pendingStream(oldSink, token) == 0` AND the streamer's buffer for that pair == 0. As written the assertion is a false assurance.

SECONDARY (new, and only correctly specifiable under the corrected rationale): document the manual recovery route in the ops runbook — a 1-wei collectNudge or an owner registerStream pushes the buffer to the retired sink, and rescueERC20 recovers it from there, callable even while paused. Note that de-whitelisting the token first REMOVES the owner's registerStream lever, so drain BEFORE de-whitelisting.
TERTIARY: add a step 0 to the SYA ops-ordering NatSpec (:82-90) — drain the old (sink, token) stream before repointing. Unchanged from the classifier's original recommendation and still correct.
escalationTriggers: REOPEN AT MEDIUM if the old sink can ever reach a state where rescueERC20 is unavailable — ownership renounced, or the sink self-destructed/upgraded away. Not evidenced at f704130; retirement as scripted leaves the contract intact and owner-controlled.

REOPEN AT MEDIUM if a retirement procedure is adopted that revokes the shared owner's control of the retired sink as part of decommissioning, since that removes the rescueERC20 endpoint that this Low depends on.
revisedFinding.pocDisposition: test/poc-M-02-retirement-strands-buffer.t.sol MUST be retained and attached to the Low. It is the artefact that establishes both the false-assurance defect and the recovery route, and it refutes the classifier's original 'permissionless flush handles it' rationale. Retaining a PoC on a Low is unusual and correct here: two of the three positions taken on this finding were wrong, and the PoC is what settles it. Its refutation tests (R1/R2/R3) are as load-bearing as its positive tests and must not be trimmed.

auditorStatement: I raised L-02 to Medium on a claim of permanent fund destruction, commissioned a PoC to prove it, and the PoC refuted it. The raise is withdrawn without reservation. My error was concluding 'unrecoverable' from an enumeration of the streamer's external surface without checking the transfer direction inside the settle helper that three of those four functions call — and the evidence correcting me was in the Tier-3 document I had already read and mis-parsed. The finding nonetheless emerges stronger and better specified than either prior position held it: the false-assurance defect is real and was proven more sharply than I filed it, the classifier's original Low rationale is refuted, and the recommendation is now correctly scoped. I stand behind 0 High, 1 Medium, 7 Low, 1 QA. M-01 is unaffected and I confirmed that by re-examination rather than assumption — the brick reverts at the registration check before any settle is reached, so the push semantics cannot reach it.
